riskToHumans.metaTitle: Risk to humans — what harmless, moderate, and high mean
riskToHumans.metaDescription: Georgia’s reptiles are labelled harmless, moderate, or high risk to people. What each level means, which species it covers, and what to do if you meet one.

riskToHumans.title: Risk to humans
riskToHumans.subtitle: There are three levels of risk to people: harmless, moderate, and high. Below is what each one means — and what to do if you meet the animal.
riskToHumans.scaleTitle: A field label, not a medical diagnosis
riskToHumans.scaleLead: The badge on a species page shows the medical risk to people in Georgia. It is not a lab ranking of venom potency, not a measure of how “aggressive” the animal is, and not the same as conservation status.
riskToHumans.scaleDisclaimer: Educational information — not emergency medical advice. If bitten, call 112.
riskToHumans.scaleHighBody: A bite can cause severe local and systemic illness. Keep distance. If bitten, this is an emergency.
riskToHumans.scaleModerateBody: Venomous, with a lower typical profile than the highest-risk vipers — a bite still needs medical care.
riskToHumans.scaleHarmlessBody: Most species here. No medically significant venom. Do not pick them up anyway — handling stresses the animal and can confuse lookalikes.
riskToHumans.HighLead: High risk means a medically serious bite: local tissue damage and possible systemic effects that need hospital care. These are not animals that hunt people. Most bites happen when someone tries to catch, kill, or move the snake.
riskToHumans.HighPoint1Body: Two vipers: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus) — Georgia’s largest venomous snake, with the highest typical venom yield — and the nose-horned viper (Vipera ammodytes transcaucasiana). Both can cause a life-threatening bite.
riskToHumans.HighPoint2Body: Do not handle it. Step back or go around. Even for a photo, do not close in. The snake will usually leave if it has a way out.
riskToHumans.HighPoint3Body: Call 112 immediately. Stay as still as you can and do not move the bitten limb. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. This information does not replace a clinician.
riskToHumans.HighSpeciesBody: Open a profile for identification, range, and encounter notes.
riskToHumans.ModerateLead: Venomous, and a bite is a medical event — but the typical outcome is assessed below the two high-risk vipers. “Moderate” is not “mild”: it still means keep distance and get care after a bite.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint1Body: Four Vipera — Caucasus, Dinnik’s, Darevsky’s, and steppe — plus one rear-fanged species, the eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus). The rear-fanged bite is usually milder; it should still be taken seriously.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint2Body: The same rule as for high risk: do not pick it up, do not corner it, do not try to move it. Distance settles most encounters.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint3Body: Call 112. A moderate-risk bite can still cause painful swelling and needs a medical assessment. Do not wait to “see if it gets worse.”
riskToHumans.ModerateSpeciesBody: Vipers first, then the rear-fanged species. Open a profile to see why its risk is not higher.
riskToHumans.HarmlessLead: No medically significant venom. This is the default for lizards, turtles, amphibians, and most snakes in Georgia. Harmless does not mean “pick it up” — and it does not mean the animal never bites if handled.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint1Body: A bite from these species is not a venom emergency. Several harmless snakes flatten the head or hiss so they look like a viper. To identify one, open the species profile and do not pick the animal up.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint2Body: Watch it and leave it where it is. Handling stresses the animal, can spread disease in amphibians, and leaves a risk of confusing a viper for a lookalike.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint3Body: Wash your hands. Amphibian skin produces mucus or defensive secretions; moving animals between ponds spreads fungal disease. A hard bite from a large harmless snake is still a wound — clean it, and seek care if it needs stitches.
riskToHumans.HarmlessSpeciesBody: Grass snakes, the smooth snake, the cat snake, and the glass lizard — these are the ones most often mistaken for vipers. Find the other harmless species with the filter.

riskToHumans.faqIntro: Short answers to the most common questions.
riskToHumans.faq1Q: What does the badge on a species page mean?
riskToHumans.faq1A: It shows the medical risk to people: harmless, moderate, or high. Clicking it brings you here, to that level. It is not IUCN status and not a score for how likely the animal is to approach you.
riskToHumans.faq2Q: Does “harmless” mean it will not bite?
riskToHumans.faq2A: No. Harmless means no medically significant venom. A large colubrid can still bite hard if handled. Several harmless snakes mimic vipers when threatened. Leave the animal where it is.
riskToHumans.faq3Q: Why is the Montpellier snake moderate if it is not a viper?
riskToHumans.faq3A: Malpolon insignitus is rear-fanged, not a viper. Risk to people is usually milder than a viper bite, but a bite is still medically significant — treat it seriously and call 112.
riskToHumans.faq4Q: Which snakes are high risk in Georgia?
riskToHumans.faq4A: Two: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus) and the nose-horned viper (Vipera ammodytes transcaucasiana). Georgia’s other vipers are moderate risk. A bite from any of them needs medical care.
riskToHumans.faq5Q: Are lizards, turtles, or amphibians ever high risk?
riskToHumans.faq5A: No. Venom risk to people applies to certain snakes. Lizards, turtles, and amphibians are harmless. Do not pick them up; wash your hands after any contact.

seo.title: How the regional atlas works
seo.p1: Georgia’s reptile assemblages change strongly from place to place. The humid Colchic forests and Black Sea coast in the west, the high mountain zone of the Greater Caucasus, and the dry eastern regions create different conditions for different species.
seo.p2: To see those differences, choose a place on the map or in the list and see which species are confirmed there by sources. Each region page brings together the species list, main habitats, notes related to venomous species, and a map. At this stage, amphibians, turtles, and many lizards, apart from the glass lizard, are not fully tied to regional maps. A regional list should therefore not be treated as the complete fauna of a place.

about.companyBody1: Reptiles.ge is an atlas of animals of Georgia. Herpetofauna is the deep layer, following Tarkhnishvili et al. 2026. Birds, mammals, spiders, scorpions, and insects are covered more thinly in the same catalog. The site is published in four languages; Georgian is the canonical text.
about.companyBody2: We do not invent administrative regions, measurements, IUCN category, or national Red List status. Candidate taxa stay candidates.
about.companyBody3: The atlas is an editorial compilation. Photos always carry a credit; Georgia-field verification is marked only with evidence. Corrections go through the contact page.

seo.reptilesP1: Georgia sits between the Black Sea, the Greater Caucasus, and the arid east — a short geographic span that supports vipers of high mountains and Colchic forests, water snakes of rivers and wetlands, racers of dry foothills, and a widespread legless lizard often mistaken for a snake. Reptile profiles here carry Georgia-specific range notes and field photography.
seo.reptilesP2: Species richness here is shaped by elevation, humidity, and refuge habitats. Western Colchic landscapes favor moisture-linked snakes such as Natrix; eastern semi-arid basins hold Macrovipera lebetinus and fast colubrids; the subalpine belt holds mountain vipers such as Vipera dinniki, which the Tarkhnishvili et al. 2026 checklist marks as a candidate taxon. This section is about reptiles — snakes, lizards, and turtles.
seo.amphibiansP1: Frogs, toads, newts, and the Caucasian salamander sit in the same catalog, with dedicated guides. This is not a complete national list — only published profiles.
seo.birdsP1: Bird profiles follow the same rule: named sources, and a range only where a source names the region. The list is growing and does not replace the national avifauna checklist.
seo.mammalsP1: Mammal pages use the same profile structure. Few are published yet — absence from this catalog does not mean the species is absent from Georgia.
seo.spidersP1: Spider pages follow the same rule: named sources, and a range only where a source names the region. The list grows with new profiles when a sourced page is ready.
seo.venomousP1: Only a minority of Georgia’s snakes are medically significant. A species counts as venomous when it poses a moderate or high risk to humans: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus), Caucasus viper (Vipera kaznakovi), Dinnik’s viper (Vipera dinniki), nose-horned viper (Vipera ammodytes transcaucasiana), Darevsky’s viper (Vipera darevskii), and steppe viper (Vipera renardi), plus the eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus), a rear-fanged species that is not a viper. The Tarkhnishvili et al. 2026 checklist marks the Caucasus viper and Dinnik’s viper as candidate taxa. Most other snakes here — grass snake, dice snake, racers, smooth snake, cat snake — are harmless to people, though several are frequently misidentified.
seo.venomousP2: Safe encounter practice is simple: do not handle wild snakes, keep distance, and learn the lookalikes common in your region. Open each profile for identification traits, habitat, and conservation status. This is educational natural-history guidance, not emergency medical advice.
seo.venomousGuideCta: Full guide: venomous snakes in Georgia
seo.regionsP1: Distribution is recorded by Georgia’s administrative regions as a practical field layer — from Abkhazia and Adjara on the humid west to Kakheti and Kvemo Kartli in the dry east, plus the capital district of Tbilisi. A species may appear in several regions; species tied to particular elevations or habitats are more narrowly placed.
seo.regionsP2: Use the map to move from place to fauna, then open regional pages for habitats, safety notes, and the local species list. For research-grade occurrence data, profiles also cite databases such as GBIF and the Reptile Database alongside IUCN assessments where available.

venomousSnakes.subtitle: Georgia’s six medically significant vipers plus the rear-fanged eastern Montpellier snake — with identification marks, risk, and regional range. Open a species profile and learn how to act safely during an encounter.

venomousSnakes.speciesBody: Georgia has 7 venomous snakes with moderate or high risk to humans — six vipers and one rear-fanged species. Each profile includes identification marks, range, and the main safety rules.
venomousSnakes.mostVenomousTitle: Which is the most venomous snake in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.mostVenomousBody: The <giurza>Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus)</giurza> is Georgia’s largest high-risk venomous snake. The nose-horned viper is also high risk. The other vipers are moderate risk.
venomousSnakes.vipersBody: Georgia has six medically significant vipers: the <giurza>Levantine viper</giurza> and five species in the genus Vipera. Western Georgia’s humid Colchic forests are home to the <kaznakovi>Caucasus viper (Vipera kaznakovi)</kaznakovi>, whose risk to people is moderate.
venomousSnakes.rearFangedBody:
The <malpolon>eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus)</malpolon> is a rear-fanged species with moderate risk to people.

The <telescopus>cat snake (Telescopus fallax)</telescopus> is also rear-fanged, but it is harmless to people — its venom is mainly used to subdue prey and does not present a significant medical risk to humans.

Neither of them is a viper. If bitten by a moderate-risk species, call 112 and read the <bite>snakebite guide</bite>.
venomousSnakes.safetyTitle: What to do if you meet one
venomousSnakes.safetyLead: Most snakes do not attack people unless they feel threatened. In most cases, staying calm, keeping a safe distance, and giving the snake a way out is enough.
venomousSnakes.safetyDisclaimer: This information is educational and is not an emergency medical instruction. If a snake bites you, call 112 immediately.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep1Body: Do not catch, touch, or try to move a wild snake — bite risk rises exactly in those situations.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep2Body: Go around the snake or calmly step back. Keep a safe distance and do not approach even to take a photo.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep3Body: Many harmless snakes look like vipers. Killing them damages the natural ecosystem, so do not touch or kill the snake.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep4Body: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm and try to move the bitten arm or leg as little as possible. Do not cut the bite and do not apply a tight tourniquet. This information is educational and does not replace a doctor’s advice.
venomousSnakes.hikingTitle: Hiking in Georgia: which vipers live where
venomousSnakes.hikingLead: Each venomous snake in Georgia keeps to its own habitat and elevation. Knowing the zone you are walking through tells you which species you might meet.
venomousSnakes.hikingZone1Body: The <giurza>Levantine viper</giurza> lives in dry, stony and rocky places, including Shiraki, Gareji and the lower Iori, Mtkvari and Alazani, up to about 1,500 m. The rear-fanged <malpolon>eastern Montpellier snake</malpolon> keeps to dry open country in the south-east.
venomousSnakes.hikingZone2Title: Steppe in Kakheti and Shida Kartli
venomousSnakes.hikingZone2Body: The small <renardi>eastern steppe viper</renardi> is rare in Georgia. It prefers open steppe, meadows, scrub and rocky foothills, mostly at low to mid elevations.
venomousSnakes.hikingZone3Title: Damp Colchic forests in the west, up to about 1,000 m
venomousSnakes.hikingZone3Body: The <kaznakovi>Caucasus viper</kaznakovi> lives at forest edges, in ravines and in other damp, wooded places of Colchis.
venomousSnakes.hikingZone4Body: <dinniki>Dinnik’s viper</dinniki> lives in mountain meadows, near the upper edge of the forest and in rocky places. In the high mountains it is usually active from mid-April to the second half of September.
venomousSnakes.hikingZone5Body: The <transcaucasiana>nose-horned viper</transcaucasiana> lives on dry, rocky slopes around Meskheti, Trialeti and the upper Mtkvari. Higher up, above 2,000 m, <darevskii>Darevsky’s viper</darevskii> lives in rocky high-mountain meadows, including the Abul-Samsari and western Trialeti ranges.
venomousSnakes.hikingTrailBody: Watch where you step and where you put your hands, especially on rocks and in tall grass. If you see a snake, stop, step back and let it leave. Do not try to move it or get close for a photo.
venomousSnakes.hikingNote: If a snake bites you, call 112 at once. This information is educational, not first-aid instruction. See the <bite>snakebite guide</bite>.
venomousSnakes.yardTitle: How to get snakes out of the yard
venomousSnakes.yardBody: Preventing snakes from appearing in the yard mostly means reducing hiding places and controlling food sources. Many common “repellent” methods are not effective. Practical steps and safety rules are collected in a separate guide.
venomousSnakes.idBody: A vertical pupil and triangular head often point to vipers, but the rule is not universal. Similar species have a separate guide.
venomousSnakes.biteBody: Educational first steps: call 112. Do not cut or suck the bite, and do not apply a tourniquet.
venomousSnakes.lookalikesTitle: Species often mistaken for venomous snakes
venomousSnakes.lookalikesBody:
Grass snakes, smooth snakes, and other fast harmless species are often mistaken for venomous snakes.

The <telescopus>cat snake</telescopus> is rear-fanged, but it is harmless to people and is sometimes mistaken for a viper. The <malpolon>Montpellier snake</malpolon> is also rear-fanged, but it is a moderate-risk species — it is not the <giurza>Levantine viper</giurza>.

For accurate identification, compare species profiles, external traits, and range.
venomousSnakes.relatedGuidesBody: To identify a species, use the snake index, regional range maps, and the largest snakes guide. They help you tell similar species apart.
venomousSnakes.faqIntro: Short answers about Georgia’s venomous snakes.
venomousSnakes.faq1Q: How many venomous snakes are there in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.faq1A:
Georgia has six medically significant vipers: the <giurza>Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus)</giurza>, nose-horned viper, Caucasus viper, Dinnik’s viper, Darevsky’s viper, and steppe viper.

In addition, the <malpolon>eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus)</malpolon> is a rear-fanged species with moderate risk, although it is not a viper.
venomousSnakes.faq2Q: Which venomous snake is the most dangerous?
venomousSnakes.faq2A:
The <giurza>Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus)</giurza> is Georgia’s largest high-risk venomous snake. Its bite can cause severe envenoming and may become life-threatening.

The nose-horned viper is also high risk, while the Caucasus, Dinnik’s, Darevsky’s, and steppe vipers are moderate risk.

The <malpolon>Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus)</malpolon> is rear-fanged and is not the Levantine viper — it differs both in fang position and in risk to humans.
venomousSnakes.faq3Q: Where do venomous snakes occur in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.faq3A:
The Levantine viper is found mainly in dry, rocky parts of eastern Georgia; the Caucasus viper in western humid Colchic forests and the coastal zone; Dinnik’s viper in the high Greater Caucasus; the nose-horned viper in the Meskheti–Trialeti and Lesser Caucasus dry zones; Darevsky’s viper in the Javakheti–Erusheti highlands; and the steppe viper on the Javakheti plateau and in eastern steppe habitats.

You will find exact administrative regions and range maps on each species profile and in the regional atlas. If no region is given for a species, that means there is no data yet, not that the species does not occur in Georgia.
venomousSnakes.faq4Q: How do I tell a venomous snake from a harmless one?
venomousSnakes.faq4A:
Vipers often have a vertical pupil and a relatively broad head distinct from the neck, while many harmless snakes have a round pupil. But relying only on these marks is not reliable: light, viewing angle, and defensive flattening can mislead.

For example, the <giurza>Levantine viper</giurza> and <malpolon>Montpellier snake</malpolon> are often confused. It is more reliable to evaluate several traits together — body shape, color pattern, head structure, habitat, and range — and then compare species profiles.
venomousSnakes.faq5Q: What should I do if bitten?
venomousSnakes.faq5A:
Call 112 immediately and read the <bite>snakebite guide</bite>. Stay calm and try to move the bitten arm or leg as little as possible.

Do not cut the bite, do not try to suck out venom, and do not use a tight tourniquet or other home “treatment”. This information is educational and does not replace a doctor’s advice.

venomousSnakes.mythsTitle: Common errors online and in AI answers
venomousSnakes.mythsLead: Media, tourist pages, and AI answers often contain incorrect snake counts, outdated scientific names, or species mixed together. Below are the most common mistakes and their corrections.
venomousSnakes.myth1False: Myth: Georgia has only three or four venomous snakes.
venomousSnakes.myth1True: Reality: Georgia has six vipers that are medically significant for humans. Two rear-fanged species add to them: the Montpellier snake is moderate risk, while the cat snake is harmless to people. Short or outdated articles often give an incomplete count of venomous snakes in Georgia.
venomousSnakes.myth2False: Myth: Georgia’s nose-horned viper is a separate species, Vipera transcaucasiana.
venomousSnakes.myth2True: Reality: Georgia’s nose-horned viper is a subspecies of Vipera ammodytes, V. a. transcaucasiana. Older sources and the 2009 IUCN assessment list it as a separate species, Vipera transcaucasiana. Both names refer to the same snake, so it is not counted twice.
venomousSnakes.myth3False: Myth: The Montpellier snake is the Levantine viper (gyurza).
venomousSnakes.myth3True: Reality: Malpolon insignitus is a rear-fanged snake with moderate risk to people. Macrovipera lebetinus — the Levantine viper — is a front-fanged viper and belongs to the high-risk category. To tell them apart, compare both species profiles.
venomousSnakes.myth4False: Myth: A vertical pupil or triangular head always means venomous.
venomousSnakes.myth4True: Reality: These marks often point to vipers, but relying on them alone is not reliable. Light, viewing angle, and defensive flattening can change the snake’s appearance and mislead you. Evaluating several species traits and habitat together is much more reliable than identifying by one rule.

whatIs.title: What is a turtle?
whatIs.p1: A turtle is a reptile in the order Testudines, best recognised by a shell that is part of its body. In everyday language, “turtle” can refer to a land tortoise, a freshwater turtle, or a sea turtle, but all share the same basic plan: a shell, a horny beak, and reproduction by eggs.
whatIs.p2: Turtles are not lizards or amphibians. They are a separate reptile lineage: some live fully on land, some are tied to ponds and rivers, and sea turtles are adapted to marine life. Georgia’s turtles are land and freshwater species; sea turtles are not among Georgia’s ordinary local species.

shell.title: The turtle shell and body structure
shell.p1: A turtle’s shell is part of its body. From outside it looks like a hard protective shield, but inside it is connected to the spine and ribs. A turtle cannot leave its shell. The short answer to “can a turtle come out of its shell?” is no: it is body, not a house.
shell.p2: The upper part of the shell is called the carapace. That is the shield we see from above. The lower part is the plastron — the shield on the belly side. Together they protect the body and vary among species in shape, height, and pattern.
shell.p3: Turtles do not have teeth; they cut or tear food with strong jaws and a horny beak. Land tortoises usually have stronger, column-like legs for walking. Freshwater turtles often have webbed feet, while sea turtle limbs look like flippers. These differences reflect how they live, although one sign alone is not always enough to identify a species.

types.title: Land, freshwater, and sea turtles — what is the difference?
types.intro: Turtle groups differ mainly by habitat and movement. These traits are useful first clues, but not absolute rules: shape, colour, and behaviour vary among species.

land.habitat: Land: steppe, scrub, dry open areas, and other terrestrial habitats.
land.shell: Often higher and dome-shaped, though shape depends on the species.
land.limbs: Strong legs and claws; swimming webs are usually not a key feature.
land.adaptations: Walking on land, digging, and moving through terrestrial vegetation.

freshwater.habitat: Ponds, lakes, wetlands, old channels, and slow waters.
freshwater.shell: Often lower and flatter, which helps movement in water.
freshwater.limbs: Often webbed feet; they can also come onto banks.
freshwater.adaptations: Swimming, basking on banks or vegetation, and laying eggs on land.

sea.habitat: Seas and oceans; they come ashore to lay eggs.
sea.shell: Usually smoother and adapted for moving through water.
sea.limbs: Flipper-like limbs instead of walking feet.
sea.adaptations: Long-distance swimming; movement on land is comparatively awkward.

types.outro: Georgia’s turtles are <land>land</land> and <freshwater>freshwater</freshwater> species. Sea turtles are not among Georgia’s ordinary local turtles.

diet.title: What does a turtle eat?
diet.p1: There is no single universal answer to “what does a turtle eat?” Diet depends on species, age, and environment. Land tortoises often eat plant material — grasses, leaves, flowers, and other soft vegetation. That does not mean every species feeds in exactly the same way.
diet.p2: Freshwater turtles often use a wider range of food: invertebrates, small aquatic animals, carrion, or plant material depending on the species and age. Sea turtle diets also differ: some are associated with jellyfish, others with seagrass or other marine organisms. Feeding a wild turtle in nature is not needed and can cause harm.

lifespan.title: How long does a turtle live?
lifespan.p1: Turtle lifespan cannot be reduced to one number. It depends on species, size, environment, food, predators, disease, and whether the animal lives in the wild or under human care. Many turtles are associated with long lives, but that does not mean every turtle lives for 100 years.
lifespan.p2: Large land tortoises and some sea turtles are often linked with longer lifespans, while smaller species or turtles in riskier environments may live much less. For a specific species, it is better to rely on its profile, a reliable scientific source, or a conservation assessment rather than a general myth.

reproduction.title: How do turtles reproduce?
reproduction.p1: Turtles are egg-laying animals. Turtle reproduction is tied to land in the sense that turtle eggs are not left in the water: freshwater turtles and sea turtles also come onto a bank or beach to lay eggs.
reproduction.p2: The female digs a turtle nest in soil, lays the eggs, and covers them. Hatching time, nest site, and clutch size differ among species, so one number cannot be correct for all turtles. Hatchlings leave the nest on their own and move toward suitable habitat.

testudo.habitat: Dry open terrestrial habitats — steppe, scrub, semi-desert, and open woodland edge.

emys.traits: Low oval shell; dark background with yellow dots or short streaks; no broad red stripe behind the eye.
emys.habitat: Still or slow freshwaters — ponds, lakes, wetlands, old channels, and slow rivers.
emys.conservation: IUCN: NT; not included in Georgia’s 2014 Red List.

mauremys.traits: Relatively flat shell; often pale lengthwise stripes on the neck; no broad red stripe behind the eye.
mauremys.habitat: Ponds, lakes, and slow freshwater bodies.

trachemys.traits: T. s. elegans often has a broad red stripe behind the eye; relatively flat shell; webbed feet.
trachemys.habitat: Lakes, ponds, and other freshwater bodies; breeding populations are known near Tbilisi and Batumi.

georgiaComparison.note: External appearance alone is not always enough for exact identification. In uncertain cases, use the <identify>turtle identification</identify> guide and compare several traits together.

conservation.title: Turtle conservation in Georgia
conservation.p1: Georgia’s native turtles are the Mediterranean tortoise, European pond turtle, and Caspian turtle. Of these, the Mediterranean tortoise is listed as Vulnerable (VU) in Georgia’s Red List. For this species, and for wild turtles in general, key problems include habitat loss, changes to wetlands and banks, road mortality, and removal of individuals from nature.
conservation.p2: Wild turtles should not be taken home or moved elsewhere. That can harm the animal and local populations. The red-eared slider is an introduced species in Georgia. Releasing a pet slider into nature is not a solution: it may start a new population, compete with native freshwater turtles, and affect the ecosystem. If the legal side matters, check a current official source.

turtles.faqIntro: Short answers to the most common questions.
turtles.faq1Q: How many turtle species are there in Georgia?
turtles.faq1A: Four turtle species occur in Georgia: the Mediterranean tortoise, European pond turtle, Caspian turtle, and the introduced red-eared slider.
turtles.faq2Q: Which turtles are native in Georgia?
turtles.faq2A: Three are native: Mediterranean tortoise (Testudo graeca), European pond turtle (Emys orbicularis), and Caspian turtle (Mauremys caspica). The red-eared slider is introduced.
turtles.faq3Q: Which turtles are land turtles and which are water turtles?
turtles.faq3A: Only the Mediterranean tortoise is terrestrial. Pond, Caspian, and red-eared slider turtles are freshwater species.
turtles.faq4Q: How do I tell turtle species apart?
turtles.faq4A: Start with land vs water, then shell and head marks. Full comparison is on the <identify>turtle identification</identify> guide; concrete traits are on each species profile.
turtles.faq5Q: Where do turtles occur in Georgia?
turtles.faq5A: The land tortoise lives in open, dry places; water turtles live in ponds and wetlands. Confirmed regions are on each species profile and in the regional atlas.
turtles.faq6Q: How do I recognise a red-eared slider?
turtles.faq6A: T. s. elegans often has a broad red stripe behind the eye; native water turtles lack that mark. It is an introduced species; details are on its profile.
turtles.faq7Q: What is the difference between the pond turtle and the Caspian turtle?
turtles.faq7A: Both are native freshwater turtles from different families. The pond turtle is in Emydidae; the Caspian turtle is in Geoemydidae. Field marks and range are on their profiles.
turtles.faq8Q: Can I take a turtle home?
turtles.faq8A: Do not take wild turtles home: collection harms populations, and taking a Mediterranean tortoise from nature or trading it is restricted by law. Watch it, take a photo and compare the marks in the ID guide. Then leave the turtle where you found it.

snakeIdentify.metaTitle: How to tell venomous from harmless snakes in Georgia
snakeIdentify.metaDescription: How to tell venomous from harmless snakes in Georgia: compare the Levantine viper, Caucasus viper, water snakes, Montpellier snake, and glass lizard.
snakeIdentify.keywords: venomous vs harmless snake Georgia, how to identify venomous snake, viper vs grass snake, glass lizard vs snake
snakeIdentify.heroImageAlt: Venomous viper in forest and harmless grass snake by a stream — comparison
snakeIdentify.title: Venomous or harmless?
snakeIdentify.subtitle: Most snakes in the Republic of Georgia are harmless. A vertical pupil and a broad, triangular head occur in some venomous snakes, especially vipers, but neither cue on its own is enough for reliable species identification.
snakeIdentify.guideP1: Telling a venomous snake from a harmless one by photo alone is not always reliable. It is better to consider several cues together: appearance, habitat, region of Georgia, and similar species.
snakeIdentify.guideP2: Common mix-ups and practical cues make identification easier, but they do not replace guaranteed field identification. It matters most to recognize the Levantine viper and the <kaznakovi>Caucasus viper (Vipera kaznakovi)</kaznakovi>, as well as the other venomous species. Many harmless racers, the smooth snake, and the glass lizard are also often mistaken for venomous snakes. The full list of venomous species is in a separate guide: <venomous>venomous snakes in Georgia</venomous>.
snakeIdentify.signsTitle: What people often check — and why one cue is not enough.
snakeIdentify.signsWarning: No external mark on its own proves that a snake is venomous. If you are not sure of the species, keep a safe distance and compare several cues in the species profiles.
snakeIdentify.sign1Body: Vipers often have a vertical pupil, while many harmless snakes have a round one. But pupil shape is not always easy to see, especially from a distance or in poor light. Also, a vertical pupil is not limited to venomous snakes.
snakeIdentify.sign2Body: A broad or triangular head can be typical of vipers, but harmless snakes also often flatten the head defensively. For that reason, venomousness cannot be determined by head shape alone.
snakeIdentify.sign3Body: Some harmless or lower-medical-importance species can resemble venomous snakes. For example, Dahl’s whip snake is sometimes confused with vipers, and the glass lizard is taken for a snake. In those cases, compare several cues and open the relevant species profiles.
snakeIdentify.sign4Title: When you are not sure of the species.
snakeIdentify.sign4Body: Do not catch or kill the snake. Most species in Georgia are not dangerous to people. The list of venomous snakes and related safety information is in a separate guide.
snakeIdentify.chainTitle: Levantine viper → Caucasus viper → other venomous species.
snakeIdentify.chainBody: The comparison starts with the medically important Levantine viper, then moves to the Caucasus viper, which is tied to humid forests of western Georgia, and finally to other venomous or venom-bearing species.
snakeIdentify.pairsTitle: Species that are often confused with one another.
snakeIdentify.pairsBody: Common mix-ups include racers and vipers, the glass lizard and true snakes, and the Montpellier snake and the Levantine viper. Each comparison links to the relevant detailed species profile.
snakeIdentify.faqIntro: Short answers to the most common questions.
snakeIdentify.faq1Q: How do I tell a venomous snake from a harmless one?
snakeIdentify.faq1A:
The most reliable way to identify a snake is species identification, not one visible mark. Pupil shape and head structure can help, but lighting, viewing angle, and defensive behavior can mislead.

Compare its marks, range, and habitat with the species profiles. In case of a bite, do not wait for precise species identification — seek emergency medical care first.
snakeIdentify.faq2Q: Is the glass lizard a venomous snake?
snakeIdentify.faq2A: No. The glass lizard is a legless lizard, not a snake. It has movable eyelids and external ear openings — features snakes lack. Because of its large size and long body, it is often mistaken for a snake, but it is not venomous to people.
snakeIdentify.faq3Q: Which venomous snake should I learn first?
snakeIdentify.faq3A: Start with the Levantine viper, one of the medically most important venomous snakes in Georgia. Then learn the Caucasus viper, which is tied to western Georgia’s Colchic and humid habitats and is sometimes confused with harmless snakes. The remaining species are gathered in the full venomous-snakes guide.
snakeIdentify.faq4Q: Can I identify a snake from a photo with certainty?
snakeIdentify.faq4A:
A precise snake identification from a photo is not always possible. Compare visible marks, habitat, and similar species with the species profiles.

If a snake has bitten you, do not wait for a perfect ID — seek emergency medical care. Take a photo only from a safe distance and only if doing so creates no additional risk.
snakeIdentify.ctaBody: Open a species or the venomous snakes guide. First steps after a bite are in a separate guide.
snakeIdentify.quizCtaBody: This guide is field identification. Photo practice lives on a separate quiz — ten frames, four names.
snakeIdentify.mythsLead: A single photo or casual advice is not always enough to identify a species accurately. Keep your distance and compare several cues: appearance, range, habitat, and similar species.
snakeIdentify.myth1False: Myth: A vertical pupil always means the snake is venomous.
snakeIdentify.myth1True: Reality: Many vipers have a vertical pupil, but this cue is not always easy to see and is not limited to venomous snakes. Use several cues together to identify the species.
snakeIdentify.myth2False: Myth: A triangular head necessarily means the snake is a viper.
snakeIdentify.myth2True: Reality: A harmless snake may flatten its head when threatened and look more triangular. Head shape alone is not a reliable identification mark.
snakeIdentify.myth3False: Myth: The Montpellier snake is the Levantine viper.
snakeIdentify.myth3True: Reality: The Montpellier snake (Malpolon) and the Levantine viper are different snakes. The Montpellier snake has rear fangs in the back of the mouth; the Levantine viper is a viper with front fangs.
snakeIdentify.myth4False: Myth: The glass lizard is a venomous snake.
snakeIdentify.myth4True: Reality: The glass lizard is not a snake at all — it is a legless lizard. Unlike snakes, it has movable eyelids and external ear openings. It is not venomous to people.
snakeIdentify.editorialBody: Visual cues are educational aids, not a guaranteed field method.
snakeIdentify.editorialDisclaimer: Do not touch a snake to “check” its signs. In case of a bite, seek emergency medical care immediately.

lizardCompare.faq2A: The slow worm is smaller and smoother. The glass lizard is about 1–1.35 m and has a clear side fold. Both are harmless. The slow worm is a checklist candidate.
lizardCompare.faq3A: No. The glass lizard is not venomous and is harmless to people.
lizardCompare.faq4A: Grass snakes and dice snakes are snakes often mixed up with legless lizards. They are harmless, but they are snakes.

turtleLand.title: Land turtles of Georgia
turtleLand.subtitle: Georgia has one land tortoise — the Mediterranean tortoise (Testudo graeca). Freshwater turtles have their own guide.
turtleLand.guideTitle: A domed shell, not a pond turtle
turtleLand.guideP1: Its shell is high and domed, and its legs are thick and pillar-like: those two features tell it apart from water turtles. It has no swimming webs and no teeth; the mouth ends in a horny beak. It lives on land, in dry, open places: steppe, shrubland, semi-desert and the edges of open woodland. It does not live in water.
turtleLand.guideP2: It is widespread in eastern Georgia and much rarer in the west. The eastern form is T. g. ibera; T. g. nikolskii, described from western Georgia, is rare, and opinions differ on whether it is a separate subspecies. Georgia’s 2014 Red List assesses the species as Vulnerable.
turtleLand.speciesBody: Full profile: photos, traits, habitat, sources.
turtleLand.faqTitle: What people ask about the land tortoise
turtleLand.faqIntro: Short answers to the most common questions.
turtleLand.faq1Q: How many land tortoises are in Georgia?
turtleLand.faq1A: One: the Mediterranean tortoise (Testudo graeca). It is native to Georgia. The other turtles here — the European pond turtle, the Caspian turtle and the introduced pond slider — live in and near water.
turtleLand.faq2Q: How do I tell it from a water turtle?
turtleLand.faq2A: By the shell and the legs. The Mediterranean tortoise has a high, domed shell and thick, pillar-like legs without swimming webs. Water turtles have flatter shells. The ID guide compares all four turtles side by side.
turtleLand.faq3A: Mainly in dry, open places in eastern Georgia: Kvemo Kartli, Kakheti, Mtskheta-Mtianeti, Tbilisi and Shida Kartli. It has been seen in Gori, Tbilisi, Bolnisi and Vashlovani National Park. In western Georgia it is much rarer. It has been recorded up to about 800–1000 m, though that is not a strict upper limit.
turtleLand.faq4Q: Can I keep one at home?
turtleLand.faq4A: Not one from the wild. Taking a wild tortoise from nature or trading it is restricted by law, and the species is listed in CITES Appendix II. It is Vulnerable, and collection from the wild is one of its main threats. If you find a tortoise, leave it where it is.

turtleWater.subtitle: Two native freshwater turtles and one introduced slider. The land tortoise is on a separate guide.
turtleWater.guideP1: The European pond turtle and the Caspian turtle live in ponds, lakes, marshes and slow water, and often bask on the bank. Their shells are flatter than a tortoise’s, and their feet are webbed. The pond turtle occurs in both western and eastern Georgia; the Caspian turtle is linked to the southeast.
turtleWater.guideP2: The pond slider is not native to Georgia: it turns up in the wild when pets are released or escape. Around Tbilisi and Batumi it already breeds in the wild. The easiest way to recognise it is the broad red stripe behind the eye.

turtleWater.faqTitle: What people ask about water turtles
turtleWater.faqIntro: Short answers to the most common questions.
turtleWater.faq1A: The European pond turtle (Emys orbicularis) and the Caspian turtle (Mauremys caspica). Both live in Georgia naturally. The pond slider (Trachemys scripta) is introduced: it comes from pet turtles that were released or escaped.
turtleWater.faq2Q: How do I recognise a red-eared slider?
turtleWater.faq2A: By the broad red stripe behind the eye. The form known in Georgia is T. s. elegans, the red-eared slider. The European pond turtle and the Caspian turtle have no such stripe, so if you see it, you are looking at a slider.
turtleWater.faq3A: The European pond turtle lives in both western and eastern Georgia. The Caspian turtle is linked to the southeast: it has been seen in Tbilisi, Kvemo Kartli and Kakheti. The pond slider breeds in the wild around Tbilisi and Batumi.
turtleWater.faq4Q: Can I release a water turtle into a pond?
turtleWater.faq4A: No. The pond slider is not native to Georgia, and releasing it raises the risk that it will take hold in new places. Releases do not help native water turtles either. Do not let a pet turtle go in a lake or pond.

turtleIdentify.faq2A: Do not take wild turtles home. The Mediterranean tortoise is assessed as Vulnerable on Georgia’s Red List and is listed in CITES Appendix II. The slider is a pet species, but releasing it into the wild creates new introduced populations.

snakesInYard.metaTitle: How to get snakes out of the yard: what actually works
snakesInYard.metaDescription: Snakes in the yard: there is no 100% snake repellent. Reduce shelter and food so snakes do not stay. What works in Georgia and which myths to ignore.
snakesInYard.keywords: how to get rid of snakes in the yard, snakes in the house, snake repellent, snake repellent spray, snake repellent device, snake in garden, sulfur snake myth, milk for snakes, Georgia snakes yard
snakesInYard.heroImageAlt: Grass snake (Natrix natrix), a harmless snake, in Lagodekhi
snakesInYard.title: How to get snakes out of the yard
snakesInYard.subtitle: There is no reliable method for directly “driving” a snake out of a yard. The most practical approach is to reduce the conditions that attract snakes — hiding places and food. That lowers the chance that a snake will stay in the yard for long.
snakesInYard.whyTitle: Why do snakes enter a yard?
snakesInYard.whyLead: No snake-deterrent method is 100% effective. A yard is attractive to snakes mainly because of two things — safe hiding places and food.
snakesInYard.whyShelterBody: Tall grass, dense shrubs, logs, piles of stones or building materials, and cracks in walls make good hiding places for snakes.
snakesInYard.whyFoodBody: Rodents are important food for many snakes. If mice or rats are common in the yard, it is easier for a snake to find food there.
snakesInYard.coverImageAlt: A snake on rocks near rodents and tall grass — shelter and food in one place
snakesInYard.coverCaption: A yard can become especially attractive to snakes when it has both many hiding places — tall grass, stones, logs — and food, such as rodents.
snakesInYard.actionsTitle: What can we do to make the yard less attractive to snakes?
snakesInYard.actionsLead: The goal is not to catch or kill a snake. The safer, longer-term approach is to reduce hiding places and food sources in the yard.
snakesInYard.action1Body: Cutting tall grass makes the yard more visible and reduces places where a snake can hide unnoticed.
snakesInYard.action2Body:
Tidy piles of logs, stones, old items, and building materials. Cracks in walls and structures can be safely closed after you are sure no animal is inside. Reducing dense shrubs is especially useful along yard edges.

Do not simply fill a burrow or hole if you do not know what animal uses it.
snakesInYard.action3Body: If mice or rats appear often in the yard, first address what attracts them — open food, waste, and shelters they can access. As rodents decline, the amount of food available to snakes also declines.
snakesInYard.mythsLead: Many methods are recommended for scaring snakes away, but their effectiveness is often not reliably proven. Time and resources are better spent on yard maintenance and rodent control.
snakesInYard.myth3: Snake-repellent products and sprays said to scare snakes away.
snakesInYard.myth4: A snake-repellent device: a sound or vibration unit pushed into the ground.
snakesInYard.houseTitle: A snake inside the house — what should you do?
snakesInYard.houseBody: A snake indoors follows the same rule as one in the yard: do not catch it and do not kill it. Keep your distance, move children and pets away, and leave it a way out. A repellent product, spray, or device is not a reliable fix. If you need it removed safely, contact the relevant service. If it bites, call 112.
snakesInYard.appearTitle: What should you do if a snake is already in the yard?
snakesInYard.appearBody:
Do not try to catch, kill, or move the snake by hand. That increases bite risk, and many snakes in Georgia are non-venomous.

Keep a safe distance, keep children and pets away, and leave the snake an exit. If you need safe removal, contact the appropriate service.
snakesInYard.contactBiteBody: If a snake bites you, call 112 immediately. Stay calm and try not to move the bitten limb more than necessary. Do not cut the bite, do not suck it, and do not use a tourniquet.
snakesInYard.contactAgencyBody: If you need a snake safely caught or removed from the area, do not try it yourself. Contact the appropriate service.
snakesInYard.faqIntro: Short answers to the most common questions.
snakesInYard.faq1Q: Is there a product that repels snakes 100%?
snakesInYard.faq1A:
No. There is no reliable universal snake repellent. The most effective practical approach is to reduce hiding places and food sources.

Sprays, sulfur, and similar methods do not deliver reliable results. A snake may still appear by chance in a managed yard, but it will have fewer favorable conditions for staying there.
snakesInYard.faq2Q: Why do snakes come into the yard?
snakesInYard.faq2A: Snakes often appear in yards because of shelter or food. Tall grass, logs, piles of stones, building materials, and many rodents make the area more favorable for them.
snakesInYard.faq3Q: Do milk, sulfur, or sprays work?
snakesInYard.faq3A: No. Sulfur, milk, and similar “deterrent” methods should not be treated as reliable solutions. It is better to cut tall grass, reduce hiding places, and control rodents.
snakesInYard.faq4Q: What if a snake is already in the yard?
snakesInYard.faq4A:
Do not touch the snake or try to catch it. Watch from a safe distance and leave it an exit.

In Tbilisi, for safe snake removal, you can contact the relevant animal monitoring service at 032 272 16 00.
snakesInYard.faq5Q: What if a snake bites someone?
snakesInYard.faq5A: If a snake bites you, call 112 immediately. Stay calm and avoid moving the bitten arm or leg more than necessary. Do not cut the bite, do not try to suck out venom, and do not use a tourniquet.
snakesInYard.faq6A: No. Most snakes in Georgia are non-venomous, and many are often mistakenly considered venomous. If you are not sure of the species, keep a safe distance and do not touch the snake.
snakesInYard.ctaTitle: Identify the species — don’t act on fear alone
snakesInYard.ctaBody: Yard management lowers risk. If you see a snake, the species profiles help with identification and a safer decision.

snakeQuiz.practiceTitle: How to read a snake in a still frame
snakeQuiz.practiceLead: A quiz is not a field-safety lesson. The question “venomous or harmless?” is answered by the identify guide. Here you get one frame from Georgia, four names, and time to train your eye on photos of Georgia’s snakes.
snakeQuiz.practiceP1: Start with the head. A triangular silhouette from above often recalls a viper; an oval head in profile often belongs to a harmless colubrid. Is the neck clearly narrower than the head, or is it one mass? Many harmless snakes flatten the head and “borrow” that cue in a photo. One frame is not a verdict, but it is a start: if head and neck are separate, look toward colubrids first; if the head is broad and the neck short, compare viper profiles.
snakeQuiz.practiceP2: The pupil, if you can see it. A vertical slit in Georgia often points to a viper; a round pupil often points to a harmless snake. Light changes the cue, and many field photos hide it entirely. If the eye is a blur, do not guess from the pupil alone. Scale sheen is the same trap: a wet grass snake and a dry viper can both look glossy in one crop.
snakeQuiz.practiceP3: Then the pattern. Zigzag, spots, stripes, a plain back — that is what the quiz asks you to see in a second. The Caucasus viper and the grass snake sit close in photographs: both can show a dark back on a pale ground. The split is often head shape, keeled scales, and whether a yellow collar is visible. The smooth snake and the nose-horned viper are the same trap at another angle — small, brown, against forest litter.
snakeQuiz.practiceP4: Habitat in the background (stream, rock, steppe, leaf litter) helps, but the quiz does not ask where you are standing. Field safety — marks, risk, and what not to do — has its own guide. The job here is speed of the eye — so that before you open a species profile you already know what in the frame caught you. Below are six pairs most often confused in photographs.
snakeQuiz.lookalikesTitle: Pairs that confuse a still photo
snakeQuiz.lookalikesLead: This is not field diagnosis. It is what the eye mixes in one frame — and where the quiz draws its distractor names.
snakeQuiz.lookalike1Body: The grass snake often shows a yellow collar and a round pupil; the Caucasus viper a broader head and a vertical pupil when visible. Both are often photographed in western forests.
snakeQuiz.lookalike2Body: The dice snake is usually narrower-headed, with strongly keeled scales; the Caucasus viper is often shorter, with a sharper zigzag. A stream in the background can belong to either.
snakeQuiz.lookalike3Body: The smooth snake is small, smooth-scaled, round-headed. The nose-horned viper sits in the same browns, but the head is broader and the dorsal pattern breaks differently.
snakeQuiz.lookalike4Body: Dinnik’s viper is a high-mountain animal and still matches the smooth snake in size on a photo. Look for head width and the rhythm of the zigzag, not colour alone.
snakeQuiz.lookalike5Body: The eastern Montpellier snake is long and fast, with a large eye; the Levantine viper is heavy, with a blunt snout. Size and head profile still split this pair in a photo, unless the crop is tight.
snakeQuiz.lookalike6Body: The European glass lizard is a lizard: eyelids and an ear opening. The grass snake has neither. It never appears as a quiz option — it is here so a “snake” in a photo is not always a snake.

spiderVenomous.metaTitle: Venomous spiders in Georgia? The karakurt and lookalikes
spiderVenomous.metaDescription: In Georgia, the medically significant spider is the karakurt. Argiope is not a black widow. What to check, what not to pick up, and when to call 112.
spiderVenomous.keywords: venomous spiders Georgia, karakurt, black widow, false karakurt, Argiope
spiderVenomous.heroImageAlt: Karakurt — black female with a globular abdomen
spiderVenomous.title: Venomous spiders in Georgia?
spiderVenomous.subtitle: Among the spiders compared below, the medically significant species is the [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) (Latrodectus tredecimguttatus). Argiope is not a black widow. Do not touch or pick up an unknown spider by hand.
spiderVenomous.summaryTitle: What to know in the first minutes.
spiderVenomous.summaryLead: Among the spiders compared below, the most medically important is the [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) (Latrodectus tredecimguttatus). The others are not considered a significant danger to people, although that does not mean their bites are always painless.
spiderVenomous.summary1: Do not pick up a spider. The risk of a bite rises especially when a spider is touched, pressed, or otherwise disturbed.
spiderVenomous.summary2: If you see a yellow-and-black striped spider in a large orb web, often with a white zigzag, it is probably [Argiope](argiope-bruennichi) and not a [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus).
spiderVenomous.summary3: A dark or brown spider with a reddish or yellowish band at the front of the abdomen may be the [false karakurt](steatoda-paykulliana) (Steatoda paykulliana). Colour alone cannot identify the species reliably.
spiderVenomous.summary4: Do not cut, suck, or burn the bite site.
spiderVenomous.guideTitle: Georgia’s “black widow” is not the American species.
spiderVenomous.guideP1: In Georgian-language search results, “black widow” is often associated with the American species Latrodectus mactans. L. mactans is a North American species. In Georgia, the confirmed species is the [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) — Latrodectus tredecimguttatus, which is widespread around the Mediterranean and parts of Eurasia. In older literature, Caucasian material was sometimes also listed as a subspecies of L. mactans.
spiderVenomous.guideP2: As of 2022, hundreds of spider species are known from Georgia, so the few compared here are a small part of the fauna. Specific [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) records are linked to Tbilisi, Gori, Aspindza, and the Shiraki and Eldari plains. A wide general range does not by itself confirm the species in another region.
spiderVenomous.idTitle: How do we know which spider it is?
spiderVenomous.idBody: Colour alone is not enough. Identification should consider web type, abdomen shape, size, and other traits together. If you are not sure of the species, do not touch the spider by hand and compare it with the relevant species profile.
spiderVenomous.id1Body: [Karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) and [false karakurt](steatoda-paykulliana) build a loose, irregular cobweb, often close to the ground — among stones, vegetation, and different objects. [Argiope](argiope-bruennichi) builds a large, round orb web. Its web often has a white zigzag structure called a stabilimentum.
spiderVenomous.id2Body: An adult female [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) is about 7–15 mm in body length. The abdomen is rounded and glossy black. Red spots are often visible on the back, although in adult females they may partly or completely disappear. Therefore, “thirteen red spots” are not a required mark for identifying karakurt. You also should not expect the hourglass-like mark known from the American black widow to be present.
spiderVenomous.id3Body: [False karakurt](steatoda-paykulliana) (Steatoda paykulliana) is often dark brown or almost black. It may have a reddish, orange, or yellowish band on the front of the abdomen. It is not a [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus). It has venom, and a bite can be painful. Do not touch it. Seek medical care if pain is severe or symptoms worsen.
spiderVenomous.id4Body: [Argiope bruennichi](argiope-bruennichi) stands out with bold yellow-and-black cross-bands and often sits in the centre of a large orb web. The [lobed argiope](argiope-lobata) (Argiope lobata) is paler and has distinct lobes on the sides of the abdomen. Both are orb-web spiders and are not considered a medically significant danger to people.
spiderVenomous.dontLead: Seeing a spider does not automatically mean it is a pest. Spiders feed on other small arthropods. Picking one up increases the bite risk.
spiderVenomous.dont1: Do not pick up a spider, including only “to check” or identify it up close.
spiderVenomous.dont2: You do not need to destroy every web found in a garden. For example, [Argiope](argiope-bruennichi) hunts insects and is not a black widow. If a web is not blocking people’s everyday movement, it can be left in place.
spiderVenomous.dont3: Do not cut, suck, or burn a spider bite.
spiderVenomous.speciesBody: If the spider’s traits match the [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus), check the details on its profile and do not touch the spider by hand.
spiderVenomous.mythsLead: On the Georgian internet, local spiders are sometimes described with the names of North American species or with information written about them. That makes it important to check the scientific name and the range confirmed for Georgia.
spiderVenomous.myth1False: Myth: a yellow-and-black spider seen in the garden is a black widow.
spiderVenomous.myth1True: Reality: in Georgia, a bright yellow-and-black spider seen in a large orb web in a garden is often [Argiope](argiope-bruennichi). Argiope is not a [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) and is not considered a medically significant danger to people.
spiderVenomous.myth2False: Myth: the American black widow — Latrodectus mactans — lives in Georgia.
spiderVenomous.myth2True: Reality: the corresponding species confirmed in Georgia is the [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) — Latrodectus tredecimguttatus. Latrodectus mactans is a different species associated with North America.
spiderVenomous.myth3False: Myth: a small spider cannot be dangerous.
spiderVenomous.myth3True: Reality: spider size does not determine medical significance. For example, an adult female [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) is about 7–15 mm in body length.
spiderVenomous.myth4False: Myth: every black spider is a karakurt.
spiderVenomous.myth4True: Reality: a dark colour alone is not a [karakurt](latrodectus-tredecimguttatus) mark. The [false karakurt](steatoda-paykulliana), for example, can also be almost black. Pattern, abdomen shape, web type, and other traits matter for identification. When in doubt, do not touch the spider by hand.
spiderVenomous.faqIntro: Short answers. Bite steps are on a separate guide.
spiderVenomous.faq1Q: Is there a venomous spider in Georgia?
spiderVenomous.faq1A: Yes. Among the spiders compared here, the most medically significant is the karakurt. Argiope is not considered a significant danger to people. A false-karakurt bite can be painful, but it is not a karakurt.
spiderVenomous.faq2A: No. Argiope is not a karakurt. Argiope has bold yellow-and-black bands or a lobed abdomen and builds a large orb web. Karakurt is smaller and spins a loose, irregular web, often close to the ground.
spiderVenomous.faq3A: The false karakurt has venom and its risk to people is moderate; a bite can be painful. Clinical evidence is limited: published cases describe Australian Steatoda bites, not cases of this species in Georgia. Do not pick it up. Seek medical care if pain is severe or symptoms worsen. Call 112 immediately if breathing becomes difficult or the face or throat swells severely.
spiderVenomous.faq4Q: Is the karakurt everywhere in Georgia?
spiderVenomous.faq4A: No. Karakurt has not been confirmed in every region of Georgia. Its specific records are linked to Tbilisi, Gori, Aspindza, Shiraki, and Eldari. A general statement that the species occurs in the Caucasus does not confirm its presence in every Georgian region.
spiderVenomous.faq5Q: What should I do if a spider bites me?
spiderVenomous.faq5A: Do not cut, suck, or burn the bite site. Do not try to catch the spider either.
spiderVenomous.faq6Q: Can I pick a spider up?
spiderVenomous.faq6A: No. Picking up a spider is not needed for identification and raises the bite risk. Observe from a safe distance or take a photo without touching the spider.

spiderVenomous.ctaBody: Open a species or the bite guide. First rule: do not pick it up; after a bite, 112.
